I’ve been thinking about forgetting.

Not in the tragic, worrisome way that accompanies age, but as a quiet, constant, and almost benevolent force in our lives. We tend to think of memory as the mind’s great achievement, the hard drive where we store our identities, our loves, our learned lessons. Forgetting is its failure, the entropy that erodes the edges of who we are. But I’m not so sure. I suspect forgetting is just as crucial, perhaps more so. It’s the silent, tireless janitor of the soul, sweeping up the cognitive debris so we can walk through the day without tripping over every past moment.

Think about it. Your first heartbreak. At the time, it felt like a planet-ending event. The specific cadence of their voice, the exact shade of the shirt they wore on the day you met, the last text message—these were etched into your brain with the force of a diamond-tipped chisel. The pain was a physical weight in your chest. You were certain you would carry it forever. And now? You might remember the person, the general arc of the story, but the visceral, gut-wrenching ache is gone. The memory has faded from a full-color, surround-sound film into a grainy, sepia-toned photograph. You haven't forgotten the person, but you have forgotten the feeling. And thank goodness for that. If we retained the raw, unfiltered emotional intensity of every event, we would be paralyzed. We'd be walking, weeping archives of our own past, unable to engage with the present because we'd be so profoundly haunted by it.

Forgetting is the brain’s own form of therapy. It’s not a bug; it’s a feature. It’s the mechanism that allows us to forgive, not in a grand, saintly way, but in a practical, everyday way. We forget the slight, the minor insult, the petty grievance. We forget that our partner was irritable on a Tuesday three weeks ago. We forget the argument that seemed so important at the time. This isn't amnesia; it's the slow, merciful blurring of the sharp edges of our lives. Without it, we would be prisoners of every mistake, both our own and those of others. We would be unforgiving, because we would have perfect recall of every transgression.

Our digital world, however, is at war with this natural grace. The internet never forgets. A stupid comment made at sixteen is now a permanent public record. A photo from a regrettable phase is a digital ghost that can be summoned with a few clicks. We are building a world without the safety valve of forgetting. We curate our pasts into permanent exhibitions, and in doing so, we risk losing the ability to grow, to change, to be a different person than we were yesterday. We are creating a culture of unforgiving memory, where the person you were five years ago is held as evidence against the person you are today. This is not healthy. It is a denial of the fundamental human capacity for change, which is itself built on the foundation of forgetting.

On a more mundane level, where would we be without forgetting? You would remember every single step you took on your morning commute. You would recall the exact texture of your 4,392nd bite of oatmeal. The sheer volume of sensory data would be overwhelming. Forgetting is the filter that separates the signal from the noise. It allows the important things—the name of your child, the way to drive home, the plot of a beloved book—to stand out in sharp relief. It’s the negative space in a painting that gives the subject its definition. A life of total recall would be a life of total chaos, a canvas so crowded with information that no image could ever emerge.

The act of forgetting is also the precondition for creativity. To create something new, you must have a kind of mental blank space. You need to be able to forget, for a moment, all the established rules, all the precedents, all the “ways it’s always been done.” You have to forget Beethoven to write your own symphony, forget Shakespeare to write your own play. This isn't about ignorance, but about a deliberate suspension of memory to allow for novel connections. We forget the conventional path to find our own. Great artists, great scientists, great thinkers—they are masters of a kind of selective, creative forgetting.

We fight so hard against forgetting. We take photos to capture a moment, we write journals to record our days, we keep meticulous digital calendars to schedule our lives. We are terrified of losing the data. But perhaps we’re missing the point. The goal isn't to retain everything, but to distill the essence of our experiences into a workable, meaningful narrative. We are not our memories, not in their totality. We are the story we weave from them, a story that requires editing, summarizing, and yes, forgetting.

The person who has forgotten the most is not the one with the least rich life. They may be the one who has lived the most peacefully. They have let go of the debts, real and emotional, that so many of us carry. They have released the slights and the failures. Their mind is not a warehouse crammed with every artifact of their past, but a clean, well-lit studio, where they can work on the present. Forgetting is not the opposite of remembering; it is its necessary partner. It is the art of letting go, the wisdom of the dustpan, the quiet gift of a mind that knows how to make room for the new by sweeping away the old. And I, for one, am grateful for it.
